root_cause.corrected_summary: The reported 'hang' was never a deadlock. It is a ~23 minute suite dominated by legitimate multiprocess writer-lock stress tests, which previously exceeded 900 s timeouts and was therefore misreported as a hang. No fixture leak, thread leak or deadlock was found.

primary_defect.aggravating_factor: measured while a UE4 cook (PID 5852) plus 9 ShaderCompileWorkers were saturating CPU, so subprocess scheduling was starved
primary_defect.cost: spawns (2+8+16) x 50 rounds = 1300 subprocess spawns, each with internal wait(timeout=60) guards
primary_defect.measured: TIMEOUT >240 s when run alone; the file produced 8 collected items and ZERO test results before the 240 s kill
primary_defect.what: pytest.ini registered the `slow` marker but addopts contained no -m filter, so `pytest tests/` executed the stress tests.

secondary_defect.note: Both spawn worker processes with iteration loops; neither carried a `slow` marker, so marker-based deselection could not exclude them.
secondary_defect.what: Two genuinely slow multiprocess files were never marked slow.

root_cause.summary: The 'hang' was not a deadlock. It was an unbounded multiprocess stress test running by default, plus two unmarked slow files.

the_3_failures_reclassified.corrected: All 3 are ORDER/LOAD dependent and were triggered by deselecting the stress tests. They pass both standalone and in a full suite that includes the slow tests.
the_3_failures_reclassified.diagnosis: The 1300-subprocess stress test imposes heavy load that masks timing fragility in other tests. Removing it changes scheduling enough to expose the fragility. That is a real pre-existing test-isolation weakness, but the regression surface belongs to any change that alters suite load, not to the stress test itself.
the_3_failures_reclassified.still_open: These 3 tests remain fragile to load changes. Fixing them is worthwhile but out of scope here.
